title: Anatomy of a Storm
text:
METEOROLOGICAL CASE STUDY


STATION: KTPA • 72-HOUR HURRICANE IRMA TELEMETRY BREAKDOWN

title: Anatomy of a Storm
section: What Happens When a Hurricane Strikes Tampa?
text:
What Happens When a Hurricane Strikes Tampa?
In our 10-year meteorological record of Tampa International Airport (KTPA), one anomaly stands above all others: the early morning hours of September 11, 2017. As Hurricane Irma tore northward up the Florida peninsula, the airport’s automated sensors recorded the violent physical signature of a tropical cyclone passing just miles to the east. By examining hourly barometric pressure, sustained wind speed, and precipitation together across this 72-hour window, we can observe the exact mechanics of what happens when a tropical cyclone strikes Tampa Bay.








Figure 1: Hourly meteorological telemetry recorded at Tampa International Airport (KTPA) during the 72-hour passage of Hurricane Irma (September 9–12, 2017). Top: Station barometric pressure (inHg). Middle: Sustained wind speed (mph). Bottom: Hourly precipitation (inches).






The Barometric Engine
Under ordinary conditions, atmospheric pressure across Tampa Bay hovers around a stable 30.10 inHg (1,019 hPa). As Irma’s circulation approached the Florida Keys on September 9, KTPA’s barometer began a steady, steep descent. By 2:00 AM on September 11, the barometer plummeted to a decade-low record of 28.69 inHg (971.5 hPa). This precipitous V-shaped drop created a steep pressure gradient across western Florida, essentially turning the skies above Tampa into a giant atmospheric siphon that drew in gale-force winds from hundreds of miles away.


Wind and Rain in Lockstep
The middle and bottom panels reveal how closely winds and rainfall sync with barometric collapse. As the pressure bottomed out during the early hours of September 11, sustained winds surged from calm 5–10 mph sea breezes into tropical storm-force gales of 41 to 46 mph, with violent squall gusts recorded up to 66 mph. Simultaneously, heavy spiral rain bands dumped torrential precipitation over Hillsborough County, dropping over 4.5 inches of rain in just a few concentrated hours before the storm center moved north toward Georgia.


The Broader Lesson: Why Storm Track Dictates Tampa Bay’s Fate
What makes Hurricane Irma’s signature particularly revealing is how track geography dictates Tampa Bay’s vulnerability. Because Irma tracked just inland to the east of Tampa, the storm’s counterclockwise rotation drove surface winds out of the northeast and east. These offshore winds pushed bay water outward into the Gulf of Mexico, causing a dramatic “negative storm surge” that temporarily drained the bay floor instead of flooding coastal neighborhoods.
By contrast, when Hurricane Helene (September 2024) passed offshore in the Gulf to the west, and Hurricane Milton (October 2024) made landfall just south near Siesta Key, their counterclockwise winds blew onshore into Tampa Bay. That onshore push, combined with historic rainfall (Milton dumped 16.03 inches at KTPA), transformed that same atmospheric pressure collapse into devastating coastal storm surge. The data confirms that while barometric drop dictates storm intensity, it is the storm’s track relative to Tampa Bay that determines whether water is drained away or driven ashore.

title: Records
section: Detailed Profiles of Each Record Extreme
text:
Detailed Profiles of Each Record Extreme





🌡️ All-Time High Temperature: 98.0°F


August 11, 2023 • 10-Year Average High: 83.2°F


During the peak of the 2023 persistent subtropical ridge, temperatures at Tampa International Airport climbed to 98.0°F—nearly 15°F above the 10-year average daily high (83.2°F) and marking the hottest single reading across the entire 10-year observational period. Combined with a dew point near 80°F, heat index values exceeded 115°F.








❄️ All-Time Low Temperature: 29.0°F


December 24, 2022 • 10-Year Average Low: 68.3°F


A historic arctic outbreak drove sub-freezing polar air deep into peninsular Florida on Christmas Eve 2022. KTPA bottomed out at 29.0°F—almost 40°F colder than the typical 10-year average low (68.3°F), recording a hard freeze and setting the coldest temperature of the 2015–2024 decade.








💧 Peak Atmospheric Dew Point: 82.0°F


August 7, 2024 • 10-Year Average Dew Point: 64.2°F


Dew points exceeding 75°F are considered oppressive; on August 7, 2024, deep tropical moisture over Tampa Bay surged the dew point to 82.0°F, nearly 18°F above the 10-year baseline average (64.2°F). This saturated atmosphere trapped heat at ground level and delivered record atmospheric moisture content.








🌪️ Lowest Barometric Pressure: 28.69 inHg


September 10, 2017 • 10-Year Average Pressure: 30.04 inHg


As Hurricane Irma tracked northward through the Florida peninsula, its central core induced a dramatic atmospheric pressure collapse. KTPA’s barometer plummeted from its typical 30.04 inHg baseline down to 28.69 inHg (971.5 hPa), the lowest barometric pressure recorded in the 10-year period.








💨 Peak Sustained Wind: 47.0 mph


September 10, 2017 • 10-Year Average Peak Wind: 13.5 mph


The strongest 2-minute sustained wind speed recorded across the 10-year period reached 47.0 mph during Hurricane Irma’s closest approach—more than triple the typical daily peak sustained wind (13.5 mph), accompanied by peak instantaneous wind gusts of 66 mph at airport anemometers.








🌧️ All-Time Wettest Day: 16.14 Inches


August 4, 2024 • 10-Year Average Daily Rain: 0.36 in


Slow-moving tropical moisture feeder bands associated with Hurricane Debby dropped an astounding 16.14 inches of rain in a single 24-hour observational cycle at KTPA—nearly 45 times the typical daily rainfall (0.36 in), shattering all previous 10-year daily rainfall records.

title: About the Project & Author
section: The Spark: A Lifelong Fascination with Weather
text:
The Spark: A Lifelong Fascination with Weather
Ever since I was little, my parents would constantly find me sitting in front of the TV, completely captivated by weather reports. While other kids were watching cartoons, I was drawn to the radar loops, the satellite views, and the meteorologists tracking cold fronts, squall lines, and tropical systems.
That fascination naturally followed me into the classroom. Throughout science classes in late elementary and early middle school, I was always asking why—trying to understand what drove high and low pressure, what created thunderstorms, and how the atmosphere operated. Outside of class, I dove into independent research and study, reading whatever I could find about atmospheric science and meteorology.
When the opportunity came to build this final project as a Junior at New College of Florida, choosing Tampa Bay’s weather was a natural extension of a lifelong passion that started in my childhood living room.

title: About the Project & Author
text:
Data & Methods

Primary Historical Dataset: 10 years (2015–2024) of hourly surface meteorological records from the automated station at Tampa International Airport (KTPA), sourced via NOAA’s National Centers for Environmental Information (NCEI) Local Climatological Data (LCD).
Real-Time Data: Live telemetry fetched dynamically from the National Weather Service (NWS) API.
Technology Stack: Built using R, Quarto, and the tidyverse (dplyr, ggplot2, patchwork, plotly, leaflet).

title: Natural Disasters
text:
Chronological Disaster Profiles





🌀 Hurricane Hermine


September 2, 2016 • Category 1 Hurricane


Hermine ended an 11-year hurricane landfall drought in Florida. Its outer circulation drove persistent tropical gale gusts and significant coastal inundation across southern Tampa Bay and coastal Pinellas County.








🌪️ Hurricane Irma


September 10, 2017 • Category 4 Hurricane


Irma tracked directly up the spine of the Florida peninsula, triggering the lowest barometric pressure reading of the entire 10-year period (28.69 inHg), sustained winds of 47 mph with gusts to 66 mph, and 11.7 inches of rain.








🌊 Hurricane Michael


October 10, 2018 • Category 5 Hurricane


While Michael made landfall in the Florida Panhandle as a monstrous Category 5 storm, its massive counter-clockwise wind field pulled water straight out of Tampa Bay and Hillsborough Bay, creating a rare “reverse negative storm surge.”








💨 Hurricane Ian


September 28, 2022 • Category 4/5 Hurricane


Ian initially headed toward Tampa before turning into Cayo Costa. Powerful offshore winds completely drained Tampa Bay’s seabed hours before shifting winds brought dangerous tropical storm-force gusts across the bay area.








❄️ Christmas Arctic Freeze


December 24, 2022 • Historic Polar Outbreak


A historic continent-wide polar blast surged sub-freezing arctic air across peninsular Florida on Christmas Eve. KTPA recorded a decade-record low of 29.0°F, bringing a prolonged hard freeze to agricultural and coastal zones.








🌊 Hurricane Idalia


August 30, 2023 • Category 3 Hurricane


Passing offshore through the eastern Gulf, Idalia’s storm surge coincided precisely with astronomical high tide, driving unprecedented coastal flooding along Bayshore Boulevard, Davis Islands, and Gulf beaches.








🌧️ Hurricane Debby


August 4, 2024 • Category 1 / Tropical Deluge


Debby produced the wettest 24 hours in modern Tampa history. Slow-moving moisture conveyor bands dumped 16.14 inches of rain at KTPA in a single day, causing extensive metropolitan and river basin flooding.








🌊 Hurricane Helene


September 26, 2024 • Category 4 Hurricane


Despite tracking over 100 miles offshore, Helene’s immense wind field produced a historic, catastrophic 6–7 ft storm surge that submerged coastal Tampa Bay barrier islands and low-lying coastal neighborhoods.








🌀 Hurricane Milton


October 9, 2024 • Category 3 Direct Strike


Just two weeks after Helene, Hurricane Milton made direct landfall near Siesta Key/Tampa Bay. It delivered a 16.03-inch extreme rainfall deluge, an eyewall barometric pressure dip, and hurricane-force wind gusts that tore the roof off Tropicana Field.
